My current finding is that the condition “\(S_n(\alpha)\star\beta=1\) for exactly two distinct shifts \(k\neq l\)” is equivalent to requiring that the two‑impulse function  

\[
f(n)=\mathbf 1_{\{k,l\}}(n)
\]

can be written as an **integer linear combination of translates of \(\alpha\)**:

\[
f=\sum_{t\in\mathbb Z}\beta(t)\,S_t(\alpha),\qquad\beta\in\mathcal F .
\]

Thus a shifty \(\alpha\) is precisely a length‑9 integer vector (supported on \(\{0,\dots,8\}\)) whose integer translates span a vector that has exactly two entries equal to 1 and all other entries 0. This reduction turns the original functional problem into a finite‑dimensional linear‑algebra question about integer combinations of shifted copies of a 9‑component vector.

My current finding is that the “shifty’’ condition is equivalent to the existence of integers \(k\neq l\) and a Laurent polynomial \(C(x)\in\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]\) such that  

\[
A(x)\,C(x)=x^{k}+x^{l}=x^{k}(1+x^{d}),\qquad d=l-k\neq0,
\]

where \(A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\) is the ordinary polynomial encoding \(\alpha\).  Thus \(\alpha\) is shifty iff its polynomial \(A(x)\) (up to a monomial factor \(x^{a}\) with \(a=\min\{i:\alpha(i)\neq0\}\)) divides a binomial \(1+x^{d}\) in the Laurent‑polynomial ring \(\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]\).  This reduces the original problem to counting all integer polynomials of degree ≤ 8 that are (up to a monomial) divisors of some binomial \(1+x^{d}\).

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to an integer polynomial  

\[
p(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\in\mathbb Z[x]
\]

that divides a binomial \(x^{k}+x^{\ell}\) (with \(k\neq\ell\)) in \(\mathbb Z[x]\).  Indeed, writing \(\beta\) as the reversed‑polynomial \(q(x)=\sum_j\beta(j)x^{j}\), the condition  

\[
S_n(\alpha)\star\beta=
\begin{cases}1&n\in\{k,\ell\}\\0&\text{else}\end{cases}
\]

is equivalent to  

\[
p(x)\,q(x)=x^{k}+x^{\ell}.
\]

Thus the problem reduces to counting non‑zero integer polynomials of degree ≤ 8 whose coefficients are zero outside \([0,8]\) and that are (up to a unit ±1) a monomial \(x^{e}\) times a divisor of \(x^{d}+1\) for some \(d>0\).  This reduction is the key step toward enumerating the shifty functions.

My current finding is that the “shifty’’ condition is equivalent to the existence of integers \(k\neq l\) and a Laurent‑polynomial \(B(x)\in\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]\) such that  

\[
A(x)\,B(x)=x^{k}+x^{l}=x^{k}\bigl(1+x^{\,l-k}\bigr),
\]

where \(A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\) is a polynomial of degree \(\le8\).  Hence a function \(\alpha\) is shifty iff its polynomial \(A(x)\) (allowing a factor \(x^{t}\) for some \(t\ge0\)) divides a binomial \(1+x^{m}\) (with \(m>0\)) in the integer Laurent‑polynomial ring.  This reduces the counting problem to enumerating all non‑zero integer polynomials of degree \(\le8\) that are divisors of some \(1+x^{m}\).

My current finding is that the condition “∃ β,k≠l such that Sₙ(α)⋆β=1 iff n∈{k,l}” is equivalent to the existence of a Laurent polynomial D(x)∈ℤ[x,x⁻¹] and an integer d>0 with  

\[
A(x)D(x)=1+x^{d},
\]

where \(A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\) is the ordinary polynomial encoding α (degree ≤ 8). Thus a shifty α exists iff its polynomial A(x) divides a binomial \(1+x^{d}\) in the Laurent‑polynomial ring (up to a monomial factor). This reduces the original functional problem to a purely algebraic divisibility problem.

My current finding is that a shifty function \(\alpha\) corresponds to a polynomial \(A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\) (degree \(\le8\)) for which there exist integers \(k\neq l\) and a Laurent polynomial \(C(x)\in\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]\) satisfying  
\[
A(x)C(x)=x^{k}+x^{l}=x^{k}(1+x^{d}),\qquad d=l-k\neq0.
\]  
Factoring out the smallest exponent \(a=\min\{i:\alpha(i)\neq0\}\) gives \(A(x)=x^{a}F(x)\) with \(F(0)\neq0\). The equation then forces \(F(x)\) to divide the binomial \(1+x^{d}\) in \(\mathbb Z[x]\); equivalently, \(F(x)\) must be a (possibly signed) product of cyclotomic factors of \(x^{d}+1\). Hence every shifty \(\alpha\) is exactly a monomial shift of a divisor of some \(x^{d}+1\) whose total degree \(\le8\). This reduction to “\(A\) is a divisor of a binomial \(x^{d}+1\) (up to a monomial factor)’’ is the key step toward counting all such \(\alpha\).

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to an integer polynomial p(x)=∑_{i=0}^8α(i)x^i that divides a binomial x^k+x^ℓ (k≠ℓ) in ℤ[x]; equivalently p(x)=±x^e·f(x) where e≥0 and f(x) is a divisor of x^d+1 for some d>0, with e+deg f≤8. This reduction turns the original combinatorial problem into counting all such polynomials (including the sign choice).

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to a primitive integer polynomial A(x)=∑_{i=0}^8α(i)x^i (with α(i)=0 for i<0 or i>8) that divides a binomial x^k+x^l.  Equivalently, there exist integers r≥0 and m>0 such that  

\[
A(x)=\pm x^{\,r}\,D(x),\qquad D(x)\mid(1+x^{m})\text{ in }\mathbb Z[x],
\]

and deg A≤8.  Thus every shifty α is a monomial factor x^r times a divisor of 1+x^m (a product of cyclotomic polynomials), and conversely any such divisor yields a shifty α.  This reduces the counting problem to enumerating all primitive divisors of 1+x^m with degree ≤8 (including the trivial divisor 1).

My current finding is that the shifty‑condition is equivalent to the existence of integers \(d>0\) and \(e\ge0\) such that the polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}
\]

satisfies  

\[
A(x)=\pm x^{e}f(x),\qquad f(x)\mid(1+x^{d})\text{ in }\mathbb Z[x],
\]

i.e. \(A(x)\) must be a monomial times a divisor of the binomial \(1+x^{d}\).  This follows from rewriting the convolution equation \(A(x)C(x)=x^{k}+x^{l}=x^{k}(1+x^{d})\) as \(A(x)D(x)=1+x^{d}\) with \(D(x)=C(x)x^{-k}\) and using that units in \(\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]\) are \(\pm x^{n}\).  Thus a shifty function exists iff its generating polynomial is a (signed) monomial factor of a divisor of some \(1+x^{d}\) with degree \(\le8\).

My current finding is that a function α is shifty **iff** its polynomial  

\[
P_\alpha(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\in\mathbb Z[x]
\]

can be written uniquely as  

\[
P_\alpha(x)=x^{a}\,G(x)
\]

with \(a\ge0\) and \(G(0)\neq0\), where \(G(x)\) is (up to sign) a divisor in \(\mathbb Z[x]\) of some binomial \(x^{d}+1\) (i.e. \(G\mid x^{d}+1\) for some integer \(d>0\)).  Consequently the number of shifty functions equals  

\[
\sum_{G\mid x^{d}+1,\; \deg G\le8,\;G(0)\neq0}\bigl(8-\deg G+1\bigr),
\]

the sum ranging over all (signed) polynomial divisors of \(x^{d}+1\) of degree ≤ 8.  This reduction replaces the original functional condition by a purely algebraic divisor problem.

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to a monic integer polynomial f(x) (with possible sign ±) of degree ≤8 that divides a binomial xⁿ+1 for some n>0; equivalently α’s polynomial is p(x)=±xᵉ·f(x) with 0≤e≤8−deg f. Thus the number of shifty functions equals  

\[
2\sum_{f\in\mathcal D}(9-\deg f),
\]

where 𝔇 is the set of monic divisors of xⁿ+1 (n≥1) having degree ≤8 (including the constant 1). This reduces the original problem to enumerating all such f.

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds exactly to a polynomial  

\[
A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^{i}\in\mathbb Z[x],\qquad A\neq0,
\]

which can be written as  

\[

\]

with \(a\ge0\) and \(D(x)\) a (signed) divisor of a binomial \(1+x^{d}\) for some integer \(d\ge1\); equivalently \(D(x)\) is a product of cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{\delta}(x)\) where each \(\delta\) satisfies \(\delta\mid2d\) but \(\delta\nmid d\). The degree constraint is \(a+\deg D\le8\). Thus counting shifty functions reduces to counting all distinct polynomials of the form \(\pm x^{a}D(x)\) with \(\deg\le8\) and \(D\mid(1+x^{d})\) for some \(d\). This reduction is the key step toward an explicit enumeration.

My current finding is that the only possible divisor‑polynomials \(D(x)\) (up to sign) are products of cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_n(x)\) whose indices \(n\) are even **and all have the same 2‑adic valuation**; the admissible even indices with \(\deg\Phi_n\le8\) are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_2=1:&\; n=2,6,10,14,18,30\;( \deg=1,2,4,6,6,8),\\
v_2=2:&\; n=4,12,20\;(2,4,8),\\
v_2=3:&\; n=8,24\;(4,8),\\
v_2=4:&\; n=16\;(8).
\end{aligned}
\]

A divisor \(D\) is any subset of one of these groups whose total degree does not exceed 8 (the empty subset gives \(D=1\)). Counting subsets with degree ≤ 8 yields  

- \(v_2=1\): 15 subsets,  
- \(v_2=2\): 5 subsets,  
- \(v_2=3\): 3 subsets,  
- \(v_2=4\): 2 subsets.  

Since the empty subset is counted four times, the number of distinct \(D\) is \(15+5+3+2-3=22\). Each \(D\) can be multiplied by any monomial \(x^a\) with \(0\le a\le8-\deg D\) and by a sign ±, giving the total number of shifty functions.

where \(D(x)\) is a product of cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{2^{r+1}t}(x)\) with a fixed \(r\in\{0,1,2,3\}\) and distinct odd integers \(t\) satisfying \(\sum_{t}\varphi(t)\le 8/2^{\,r}\).  Enumerating all such \(D\) yields exactly 22 distinct polynomials (including 1); each admits \(9-\deg D\) possible shifts \(a\) and two sign choices, giving  

\[
\sum_{D}(9-\deg D)\cdot2=160
\]

shifty functions. This matches a direct computer‑search of all \(\alpha\) with support in \([0,8]\).

My current finding is that the answer 266 given by Solver 0 is too large because it counts every subset of the 12 even‑order cyclotomic polynomials, but a product of cyclotomics divides a binomial \(x^{k}+x^{\ell}\) only when **all** its indices have the same 2‑adic valuation.  Subsets mixing different valuations (e.g. \(\Phi_{2}\Phi_{4}\)) never divide any \(1+x^{d}\), so they cannot arise from a shifty \(\alpha\).  Enforcing the common‑valuation condition reduces the admissible subsets to 22 distinct divisor polynomials (including 1); each of degree \(d\) gives \(9-d\) monomial shifts and a sign choice, yielding \(\sum_{D}2(9-\deg D)=160\) shifty functions.  Hence the correct count is 160, not 266.
